posts.author: Warpmind
posts.body:
Some silly notion struck me last night...
Has anyone tried (and just as importantly, has anyone succeeded in) making an Idle Game in RPG Maker?
Granted, most such games are clicker games, but it seems to me the engine should be able to handle that sort of continuous resource generation, with a slightly different interface for buying upgrades and such...
UPDATE:
The Idle Progression mechanic is, in and of itself, a piece of cake; a few lines in a common event/parallel process.
Making it interesting and/or engaging, that's the hard part.
TL;DR: It can be done, but it just might suck like a hull breach on the ISS.

Maybe I'm short-sighted, but I don't see any possible way in which gating resource generation by real-time can ever be an enjoyable or positive experience in a single-player game.

access

(To be really clear, I'm talking about "real-time" on the scale where you might be waiting for many minutes, hours, or days to get things done - when it's on the scale of
seconds
, like in an RTS game or an action battle system, it can balance out the otherwise-extreme emphasis on APM and make for good gameplay.)

It's easy and I mean very very easy once you know how.  Just use Time.now() (or better yet, Time.now().to_i to return an integer) in Ruby, or Date.now() in JavaScript, to return the number of seconds (in Ruby) or milliseconds (in JS) since Jan 1, 1970, based on the user's computer and regional settings.  In JS, you'll probably want to divide by 1000 to get a number of seconds, but it's not mandatory (you could also divide by 60000 to get a number of minutes, or 3600000 to get a number of hours).
Save that to a variable in your game - any normal variable - let's say Variable #5.  When you want to see how much time has passed, do the same calculation, save it to another Variable - let's say Variable #6 - and find the difference between the two to find out how much time has passed!  Finally, if you want to use the present time as a new "starting point" for how much time has passed the next time you check, set Var #5 equal to Var #6.
Implementation aside, I don't really see the value in this kind of game mechanic, outside of parody.  As a player, I'd much rather earn ("work for") resources in-game, assuming that "work" involves fun activities, than be handed them for the passing of real time.  I have used Time.now()/Date.now() before, but it's usually for things like setting arrows in a DDR minigame or judging a Timed Hit during battle - basically wherever it makes more sense to look at real time rather than Frames.

Yeah, I do note that most idle games use the idle resource gathering as a sort of complementary mechanic that takes over the resource building after a while.
In a JRPG, it could be interpreted as opening a bank account and gaining interest, investing in a business and receiving dividends, buying a mine and gaining a steady supply of ore or metal, and so on while the party is out adventuring.
Ideally, for a major project, it could be well employed as a means to acquire resources the player can't be arsed to gather manually (hiring more miners to get more steel for better weapons, perhaps?) or which otherwise would require an absurd amount of material grinding which, in my humble opinion, would slog down an otherwise enjoyable game.
I can see several ways the idle mechanics (whether including timetracking out-of-game or not) could work great within the frame of the narrative, and just as many pitfalls. At the end of the day, it's another tool to be considered for suitable placement, I suppose.
Noting the Javascript bit, though - that's bound to come in handy at some point.

posts.author: MiD
posts.body:
So I was thinking about this, I saw Unity is very expensive (everyone does idlers with Unity) and I know a lot about the RMMV engine.
It is almost impossible to do it using pseudocode as it would require a ton of parallel events and it would clog the system. But it's somewhat doable through scripting / custom plugins and such.
First trouble would be the menus - menus pause the $gameMap updates, so it would require to not pause them. The way it works though, it's not possible to have the Menu scene above the Map scene and to have the Map scene also working at the same time.
The offline progress is easy to bypass, as you can save the exact date and time in the savegame, and then call the current date and time when the player loads the game. As others mentioned though, this would be quite exploitable, but I assume you could take the dates and times from some server somewhere, I dunno.
You could create custom menus by click areas, by spawning rectangle sprites on the screen, and each one having its x and y, width and height, so that you know when the cursor is inside them - you would most definitely require to make classes for that.
But, if you open up a menu with a lot of sprites, the system would most likely start lagging, as each is running their own update cycle, so that it knows if it's been selected or not.
This is the main problem with an idler on RM actually, the lag.
This could be solved if you pre-made select areas, and therefore only had to draw the icons. So the entire menu would run 1 update, but it would have divided itself into clickable areas for example. Kinda like an invisible grid.
The gameplay of an idler is where you would have to get creative, of course, but a simple idler like cookie clicker would be easy to make gameplay-wise. AFAIK it was made with JS anyway.
But yeah, the lag would be something that needs to be addressed, I've had a lot of issues with it myself.

Anything is possible to bithack or bypass by taking snapshot saves, so I would not bother trying unless it's a profit impacting feature.  One thing that can be done, is to create a monitoring script that captures glide time (a running count) in the game and compares it to the clock time to detect gaps.  If detected, the game would freeze and load the most recent save.  Also, all save times could be encrypted a couple different ways and saved in different locations.  A loaded game would compare timestamps and checksums.  Failures would result in an autoload of a previous save point.  I would only let players have one save slot, but have the game autosave about every 5 minutes, keeping about 10 saves in memory.
This would likely stop universal hacks and time cheat methods, limiting it to a trickle.

posts.author: Tai_MT
posts.body:
I probably wouldn't bother with "offline progress" for it.  The only reason you'd need to care about "offline progress" is if you've got heavy monetization in the game.  If you have a singleplayer game where a player needs to wait 10 real life hours for something...
Well, you've designed your game wrong.
As for lag... I'm not really sure what you guys are planning to do to cause a ton of lag.
Couldn't you handle all "resource generation" through use of a single event and a variable for each resource?  You'd just need the system to check each variable before calling the "Else Case" of the event.  If you are tracking a crapload of resources this single check COULD get pretty hardcore and laggy... but why are you tracking more than like 5 resources, anyway?  Or, allowing insane amounts of upgrades to calculate or deliver thousands of something to the game?  Especially if it's singleplayer with no monetization?
Honestly, I'd just link a "clock" event to the resource collection.  "Every time the seconds variable is 30, calculate and deliver resources".  Then, you have no need for the computer clock, it couldn't really be exploited, and it'd just rely on game ticks.
I'm not sure how "laggy" that actually is, but a couple rudimentary tests didn't produce any visible lag on my machine.
Yeah, I tried to make an idle game in RPG Maker once upon a time.  The problem I kept running into was just that it was boring.  I got the "resource creation and delivery" to work fine, but revolving any interesting or engaging gameplay around that was a problem.
Basically, it was a "town management" type game.  You could build a structure, that structure would increase the variable for that by 1, and then the common event would just read "variable = x, give Y amount of that resource".
